Oil & gas · Tanzania · Natural gas

Gas fields, gas pipelines and the LNG host area, mapped from the air

Tanzania’s natural gas is processed in the south and carried by a high-pressure pipeline of about 551 km. Along that chain the land rules change. Upstream facilities, such as wells and upstream processing, sit inside safety zones whose extent PURA determines; transmission lines sit inside wayleaves the licensee acquires; and at the site for a planned LNG plant on the southern coast, the land title holder has completed the compensation process and the project awaits a final investment decision. Land around a site can change in the meantime. We map what stands in each, and what has changed, from dated imagery reviewed by a person.

Request a proposal See sample outputs

The gas chain, on the ground

Three kinds of land, three sets of rules

Natural gas in Tanzania moves from upstream fields through processing plants and high-pressure lines to users, and each stage sits on land protected in a different way.

Upstream · PURA

Wells and upstream processing

The Petroleum Act puts “a safety zone surrounding every facility used for carrying out petroleum activities, unless otherwise determined by PURA”, and “a person shall not carry unauthorised activity in the safety zones” (s.203(5)). The zones sit in the Part on upstream operations, so they surround upstream facilities such as wells and upstream processing.

Midstream · EWURA

High-pressure transmission lines

A licensee secures rights of way for gas pipelines, subject to the Gas Utilisation Master Plan and in consultation with EWURA (s.185), and acquires wayleaves around existing and future gas infrastructure that owners on or bordering them must not interfere with (s.186).

Land and lenders

The LNG host area

The site for a planned LNG plant on the southern coast was selected in 2013, and its land title holder has completed the compensation process. The project awaits a final investment decision, and land around a site can change while it waits.

Two regulators divide the work. PURA regulates and monitors the petroleum upstream subsector for Mainland Tanzania (Petroleum Act, s.11), and EWURA has “regulatory powers in respect to midstream and downstream petroleum and natural gas activities” (s.29(1)). Altering, removing or connecting to a pipeline or gas installation without the licensee’s consent is an offence at every stage (s.240).

Upstream

Structures inside the safety zones around wells and upstream plants

PURA determines the extent of each safety zone, and the Act forbids unauthorised activity inside it. The operator’s land and HSE teams then need to know what stands in the zone and when it appeared. We draw the zone from the facility footprints and the distances in PURA’s determination or your own licence conditions, and list each structure inside it with its distance to the facility, then compare between dated surveys.

A new field brings new wells, field pipelines, a processing plant and access roads. A dated baseline before construction, from archive imagery and a new survey, records the structures, cleared ground and tracks around each site, so later questions about what was there first have an answer.

Your own facilities are not encroachment

Well pads, field pipelines, processing plants, camps and yards are part of the asset. We record them as the operator’s installations and keep them out of the encroachment register, unless you ask for them to be listed separately.

Gas transmission

The high-pressure gas line and its wayleave

A high-pressure natural-gas pipeline (bomba la gesi asilia) of about 551 km runs from a processing plant in the south, and gas is distributed in Dar es Salaam, including compressed natural gas connections. A new line from a southern gas field to the processing plant was contracted in July 2025.

This is the closest match to our published sample, a high-pressure gas pipeline in Mozambique. The survey follows the same steps: the route in its UTM zone, the bands you set inside and around the wayleave, each structure the review confirms with its distance and band, and each 500 m stretch rated for encroachment density.

Section by section, the register gives the wayleave team a dated inventory of what stands inside the s.186 wayleave, a ranked list of stretches to visit, and, after each scheduled re-survey, what is new or gone. Fresh digging, spoil and new tracks near the line are flagged for your field teams to check.

Where gas routes run through Dar es Salaam, structures and works are dense and small, so urban stretches get the finest imagery available and the closest review.

The LNG host area

Compensated, and waiting: a dated record of any change

Between compensation and an investment decision, land around a site can change, and that gap is where land questions build up.

An imagery history since selection. From archived satellite imagery and open datasets, we document what was built, cleared or changed on and around the site, and roughly when, from the years around its selection and compensation to today. How much archive exists varies by place and year; the report says which dates it rests on.

Settlement change around the site. Year-by-year trends in built-up land around the site boundary, access routes and nearby villages show where settlement pressure is growing. A structure register on a current dated scene gives the count.

A fresh baseline for an investment decision. If an investment decision brings a lenders’ environmental and social review, one of its questions is one the imagery can answer: what stands on and around the site now, compared with the compensation record. A dated register on the day it is needed supports that review; it does not replace the census or the valuation.

Corridors to the site. If the project goes ahead, access roads and pipeline corridors to the site will need route options. Structure counts along each alternative let the land impact be weighed before a route is fixed.

Coastal land

Under the Land Act, land within 60 m of a beach or coast, or of a river bank or inland lake shore, is among the categories the Minister can declare hazardous land by Gazette notice (s.7). Along a coastline, check whether a declaration applies before a baseline is scoped.

Drone detail near gas facilities

Satellite first near plants and wells

Around wells, processing plants and valve stations, satellite screening covers the zone without anyone on site. Where a drone survey adds detail, it is subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires: an operator with a Tanzanian principal place of business and an RPAS Operator Certificate, TCAA’s authorisation for the operation and, for Category B work, a risk assessment submitted at least 14 days ahead. Plants and wells are structures, so the 50 m rule of GN 268 reg 30 applies unless TCAA approves closer work.

On an operator’s site

Fly only with the operator’s written permission and through its site security, with the launch and recovery consents of reg 86, and never over protected places. Afridrone is working towards Tanzanian drone approvals; every drone proposal names the company that will fly.

Drone law in Tanzania

Local content

Petroleum work and the local-content rules

Gas-sector licence holders, contractors and subcontractors give preference to services rendered by Tanzanian citizens or local companies, and services not available locally are supplied through a joint venture in which a local company holds at least 25 per cent (Petroleum Act, s.219). Each AfriScan proposal for gas work states which company contracts and how the proposal meets s.219. See working with AfriScan in Tanzania.

What this is, and what it is not

Onshore land only. Structures, cleared ground, tracks and excavations visible from above, reviewed by a person. Not leak detection, not a pipe-condition or integrity survey, not an offshore service, and nothing about people. See also pipeline wayleaves in Tanzania and the global oil and gas page.

Frequently asked questions

Do the Petroleum Act's safety zones apply to our gas transmission line?

No. Section 203 sits in Part VI(a) of the Petroleum Act, on upstream operations, so its safety zones surround upstream facilities such as wells and upstream processing. A transmission pipeline is protected by the wayleave the licensee acquires under s.186 and by the s.240 offences. We register structures against whichever applies, using the zone or wayleave widths you give us.

Can you keep our own facilities out of the encroachment register?

Yes. Well pads, field pipelines, processing plants, valve stations, camps and yards are part of the asset. We record them as the operator’s installations, never as encroachment, and list them separately only if you ask.

Can you find leaks from a gas line?

No. Imagery cannot show a leak or the condition of a pipe. We map what is visible at the surface around the line, such as new structures, fresh digging, spoil and new tracks, so your field teams know where to check.

What can imagery tell us about the LNG site since it was compensated?

Where archived satellite imagery exists, a history of the site and its surroundings shows what was built, cleared or changed, and roughly when, from the years around compensation to today. How much archive exists varies by place and year, and the history is not a title, tenure or valuation check.

Do you work offshore?

No. Our registers cover onshore land, meaning the gas fields’ onshore facilities, landfall sites, pipelines and plants. Offshore wells, platforms and the sea surface are outside what we map.

Can you survey gas distribution routes in the city?

Yes, from satellite imagery. Urban routes need the finest imagery and the most review, because structures are dense and works are small. Drone flights in public areas need the local authority’s permission as well as TCAA’s approvals (GN 268 of 2026, reg 117), so satellite comes first.

Send us the line, the field or the site

The route or wayleave polygon, the facility footprints and the zone widths your licence or PURA's determination sets, or the site boundary. Tell us what the record is for: operations, a new line, lenders' review or a site history. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
